entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To manage to see, hear or understand something, but only with difficulty, for example because it is dark, far away, quiet or badly written.
entries.usage: Very common with *can* and *could*, and mostly in negatives and questions: *I couldn't make out what he said.* It often takes a *wh-* clause (*make out what / who / whether*), and a pronoun goes in the middle (*I can't make it out*). Keep the object: *make out* on its own is informal for kissing.
entries.pattern: can't / couldn't make out + a noun / what … ; make it out
examples: The sign was so far away that I couldn't **make out** the street name until we were right next to it.
Can you **make out** what she's saying? The call keeps breaking up.
My grandmother's handwriting is so shaky that I could hardly **make out** her recipe for apple pie.

drill.sentence: It was dark on the porch, but I could just {{make out}} a figure standing by the gate.
drill.hint: see, but only with difficulty (not *spot* or *pick out*)

entries.related: *figure out* — understand a problem by thinking; *pick out* — recognize one thing among many; *decipher* — formal, work out the meaning of unclear writing or a code.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To describe, discuss or explain something in detail.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and presentations, and often negative when you want to avoid a long story: *I won't go into it now.* The most frequent objects are *detail* (*go into detail*, *go into more detail*), *the reasons* and *what happened*. It is neutral and works in conversation and in writing.
entries.pattern: go into + detail / the reasons / it; I won't go into it
examples: The doctor didn't **go into** much detail, but she said the surgery went well.
Let's just say our camping trip was a disaster, and I won't **go into** the part with the raccoons.
In the second half of her talk, she **went into** how the bridge was designed to survive earthquakes.

drill.sentence: My sister broke up with her fiancé, but she didn't want to {{go into}} the reasons at dinner.
drill.hint: talk about in detail (not *get into*)

entries.related: *get into* — start discussing a topic, informal; *elaborate on* — explain more, formal; *touch on* — mention briefly, the opposite of going into detail.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To intend to do something, or to expect that something will happen.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, where it is a slightly more casual version of *plan to*. It takes an *-ing* form or a noun (*plan on staying*, *plan on it*), not a *to*-infinitive. It is frequent in negatives and questions: *I wasn't planning on coming.*
entries.pattern: plan on + -ing / noun; I wasn't planning on it
examples: We're **planning on** driving to the coast this weekend if the weather holds.
How long are you **planning on** staying in Chicago?
I wasn't **planning on** buying a new car this year, but my old one finally died.

drill.sentence: We weren't {{planning on}} having a third kid, but now we can't imagine life without her.
drill.hint: intending, followed by an -ing form (not *counting on* or *thinking about*)

entries.related: *plan to* — same meaning, a little more neutral; *count on* — expect and depend on something; *intend to* — more formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To try to be elected to a public position, such as mayor, a seat in Congress or class president.
entries.usage: The standard American verb for election campaigns: *run for office / mayor / Congress / city council / reelection*. Names of offices usually take no article (*run for mayor*, not *run for the mayor*), but *the Senate* and *the House* keep theirs. British English traditionally says *stand for*, although *run for* is now common there too.
entries.pattern: run for + office / mayor / reelection; run against someone
examples: My neighbor is **running for** the school board because she's unhappy with the new bus routes.
After twelve years as mayor, she announced that she wouldn't **run for** reelection.
In sixth grade, I **ran for** class president and lost by two votes.

drill.sentence: He's thinking about {{running for}} city council next year, so he's been going to every neighborhood meeting.
drill.hint: trying to win a seat on, in an election (not *campaigning for*)

entries.related: *run against someone* — compete with a rival candidate; *stand for* — British for the same idea; *campaign for* — work to win votes or support.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To say publicly and openly what you think, especially that you oppose something, often when this takes courage.
entries.usage: Common in news and serious conversation: *speak out against bullying / harassment / a plan*. It suggests courage, because the speaker may face criticism or other risks. It has no direct object; you can also *speak out about* a problem or *speak out for* a cause.
entries.pattern: speak out against / about / for + something
examples: After the game, several players **spoke out** about the abuse they receive online.
It took courage for the nurses to **speak out against** unsafe staffing at the hospital.
Residents **spoke out** at Tuesday's meeting against plans to close the public pool.

drill.sentence: She was the only teacher who wrote to the local paper to {{speak out}} against the new testing rules.
drill.hint: state her opposition in public (not *push back*)

entries.related: *speak up* — say something, often to complain or to support someone, in a smaller setting; *blow the whistle* — reveal wrongdoing inside an organization.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To try hard and repeatedly to make something happen, especially by demanding it from the people in charge.
entries.usage: Common in news and at work: *push for change / reform / a raise / a new law*. It suggests steady pressure over time, not a single request. It also works as *push for someone to do something*: *They're pushing for the city to add bike lanes.*
entries.pattern: push for + change / a raise / a law; push for someone to do something
examples: Parents are **pushing for** a later start time at the high school so kids can get more sleep.
The union is **pushing for** a four percent raise and better health coverage.
I've been **pushing for** a dog for years, but my husband still says no.

drill.sentence: Neighbors have been {{pushing for}} a stop sign at that corner ever since a kid was hit by a car.
drill.hint: demanding again and again (not *calling for*, *asking for* or *pressing for*)

entries.related: *call for* — publicly demand, often once and formally; *lobby for* — try to influence officials; *press for* — push hard, slightly more formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become the target of criticism, attack, pressure or close examination.
entries.usage: Mostly used in news and formal speech in fixed phrases: *come under fire / criticism / pressure / attack / scrutiny*. The subject is the person or organization being targeted, and the reason often follows with *for*. *Come under fire* is the most common and is used for both real gunfire and harsh criticism.
entries.pattern: come under + fire / criticism / pressure / scrutiny (for something)
examples: The school district **came under** heavy criticism for closing three elementary schools at once.
Our goalkeeper **came under** a lot of pressure in the second half but didn't let anything in.
After the data breach, the bank **came under** scrutiny from federal regulators.

drill.sentence: The restaurant {{came under}} fire online after a customer posted a video of a mouse in the kitchen.
drill.hint: became the target of — here, of harsh criticism (not *drew*)

entries.related: *face criticism* — plainer; *draw criticism* — cause criticism; *be in the line of fire* — be the one most likely to be attacked or blamed.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be published, released or made available to the public; or, about news or a secret, to become known.
entries.usage: Used for books, movies, albums, products, results and news: *The movie comes out in May*, *The truth came out.* It has no object: the product *comes out*, and the company *comes out with* it or *releases* it. *It came out that …* is common for facts that become known.
entries.pattern: a book / movie / result + comes out; it came out that …
examples: The new superhero movie **comes out** next Friday, and the kids are already counting down.
When the test results **came out**, our school had the highest reading scores in the county.
It later **came out** that the contractor had never had a license.

drill.sentence: Her second novel {{comes out}} in March, and she's already planning a book tour.
drill.hint: gets published and goes on sale

mistake.wrong: The company is coming out a new phone next month.
mistake.right: The company is coming out with a new phone next month.
mistake.why: *Come out* has no object: the product *comes out*, or the company *comes out with* it.

entries.related: *come out with* — release a product or say something surprising; *be released* — more formal; *leak* — become known when it should have stayed secret.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To happen or develop, especially in a way that was not planned or is not fully explained.
entries.usage: Most common in questions about causes, *How did this come about?*, and with *through* or *as a result of*. It sounds a little more formal than *happen* and focuses on how something started, not only that it happened. The subject is usually a change, an idea or a situation, and there is no object.
entries.pattern: How did X come about? X came about through / because of Y
examples: How did your move to Denver **come about**? I thought you loved Boston.
The idea for the food truck **came about** during a long road trip with my brother.
Real change in the neighborhood only **came about** when residents started going to city meetings.

drill.sentence: Nobody's quite sure how the rumor {{came about}}, but by Monday the whole office believed it.
drill.hint: got its start, with no one planning it (not *started* or *began*)

entries.related: *happen* — plainer and more general; *come into being* — formal, begin to exist; *arise* — formal, used for problems and questions.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have to deal with a difficulty, opposition or a problem that blocks your progress.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports and in news: *come up against resistance / problems / a wall / a stronger team*. It suggests meeting the obstacle while you are already moving forward, often without expecting it. The obstacle always follows *against*; *run into* is a more casual near-synonym for problems.
entries.pattern: come up against + resistance / opposition / problems / a team
examples: We **came up against** a lot of resistance when we tried to change the school lunch menu.
In the semifinal, they **came up against** a team that hadn't lost all season.
On every home renovation, you **come up against** something nobody expected, like rotten beams.

drill.sentence: The plan for a dog park quickly {{came up against}} opposition from neighbors worried about noise.
drill.hint: was blocked by, along the way (not *ran into* or *met with*)

entries.related: *run into* — meet a problem, more casual; *hit a wall* — be blocked completely; *encounter* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start suddenly, used about war, fighting, fire, disease and other dangerous things that are hard to control.
entries.usage: Typical subjects are *war, a fire, a fight, an epidemic, violence, panic*, and also *applause* or *cheers*. It is intransitive and very common in news: *A fire broke out in the kitchen.* Note that *break out in* means to suddenly get a rash or a sweat, and *break out of* means to escape.
entries.pattern: war / a fire / a fight / panic + breaks out
examples: A fire **broke out** in the kitchen of a downtown restaurant late Saturday night.
A fight **broke out** in the stands during the fourth quarter, and security had to step in.
When World War II **broke out**, my grandfather was only fourteen.

drill.sentence: Panic {{broke out}} in the subway car when the lights went out between stations.
drill.hint: started suddenly and spread (not *set in* or *erupted*)

entries.related: *erupt* — break out violently, more dramatic; *flare up* — start again or get worse suddenly; *set in* — start and seem likely to continue, about bad weather or feelings.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To gradually become calmer, quieter or less strong, used about noise, wind, fire, excitement or interest.
entries.usage: Common with *the wind, the noise, the applause, the excitement, the fuss, the controversy*. It describes a slow decrease, so it often comes with *finally* or *wait for … to die down*. It has no object, and *things* is a frequent subject: *Wait until things die down a bit.*
entries.pattern: the wind / noise / fuss + dies down; wait for X to die down
examples: We waited for the applause to **die down** before we started the next song.
Interest in the story **died down** after a few weeks, and the reporters went home.
She's staying off social media until the fuss over her viral post **dies down**.

drill.sentence: We had to wait on the beach for the wind to {{die down}} before we could take the boat out.
drill.hint: gradually get weaker (not *let up* or *ease off*)

entries.related: *calm down* — become calm, mostly about people; *let up* — stop or become less intense, about rain or pressure; *subside* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become less and less common until it disappears completely, used about species, languages, customs and traditions.
entries.usage: Common in talk about nature, history and culture: *The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.* It describes a slow process over years or generations and has no object. For something destroyed quickly by an outside force, *wipe out* is the usual verb.
entries.pattern: a species / language / custom + dies out
examples: The language is **dying out** because only a few hundred elderly speakers are left.
Handwritten thank-you notes haven't **died out**, but they're definitely rarer than they used to be.
Many frog species have **died out** because of a fungus that spread around the world.

drill.sentence: My grandmother says the tradition of Sunday dinner with the whole family has almost {{died out}} in her town.
drill.hint: stopped existing, little by little (not *faded away* or *disappeared*)

entries.related: *wipe out* — destroy completely, often quickly; *go extinct* — about species; *fade away* — slowly become weaker and disappear.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To gradually become weaker and then disappear, used about the effect of a drug or about a feeling.
entries.usage: Very common with *the painkillers, the anesthetic, the caffeine, the effects*, and with feelings such as *the excitement* or *the novelty*: *The novelty soon wore off.* It is intransitive and often comes with *start to*, *begin to* or *by the time*.
entries.pattern: the anesthetic / caffeine / novelty + wears off
examples: As soon as the anesthetic **wore off**, my jaw started to hurt.
The novelty of working from home **wore off** after about a month.
I had three coffees this morning, and now the caffeine is **wearing off**.

drill.sentence: Take another pill only when the first one starts to {{wear off}}, and never more than four a day.
drill.hint: lose its effect, little by little

entries.related: *kick in* — the opposite, start to have an effect; *fade* — become weaker, more general; *wear out* — use something until it breaks, or make someone tired.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make someone extremely tired, physically or mentally.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about kids, work, travel and exercise. A pronoun must go in the middle (*The kids wore me out*), and the adjective *worn out* is very frequent: *I'm completely worn out.* With a thing as the object, *wear out* means to use something until it is damaged (*wear out your shoes*).
entries.pattern: something + wears someone out; be worn out
examples: Chasing a two-year-old around the park all morning really **wore me out**.
Long flights **wear me out** much more than they used to.
That meeting **wore everyone out** — three hours and we didn't decide anything.

drill.sentence: Let's take the dog for a long hike this afternoon; that should {{wear him out}} so he sleeps tonight.
drill.hint: make him really tired (not *tire him out*)

entries.related: *tire someone out* — same meaning, a little milder; *exhaust* — more formal; *wiped out* — informal adjective, completely exhausted.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To destroy or kill something completely, such as a population, a species, a town or a crop.
entries.usage: Common in news and history: *The storm wiped out the harbor.* It is often passive (*be wiped out by*), and a pronoun goes in the middle (*wipe it out*, *wiped us out*). The same verb is used for money and businesses: *The divorce wiped out his savings.*
entries.pattern: wipe out + a species / a town / savings; be wiped out by
examples: The hurricane **wiped out** almost every house on the south side of the island.
A fungus **wiped out** most of the American chestnut trees in the early 1900s.
A rival's cheaper app nearly **wiped us out** in our first year.

drill.sentence: The flood {{wiped out}} the only bridge into town, so supplies had to come in by helicopter.
drill.hint: destroyed so that nothing was left of it (not *washed away* or *took out*)

entries.related: *die out* — disappear slowly by itself; *destroy* — more general; *eradicate* — formal, remove a disease or problem completely.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To increase in amount, especially when unwanted things such as work, bills or problems collect faster than you can deal with them.
entries.usage: Very common with *work, emails, laundry, dishes, bills, debt, problems*, often in the progressive: *The bills are piling up.* In this sense it has no object; *pile something up* means to put things in a pile. The noun *pileup* is a crash involving several cars.
entries.pattern: bills / emails / work + pile up; keep piling up
examples: I was sick for a week, and now the emails have really **piled up**.
The dishes **pile up** in the sink whenever my roommate has exams.
Medical bills started **piling up** after his accident, and he had to borrow from his brother.

drill.sentence: If you don't open your mail for a month, the late fees will just keep {{piling up}}.
drill.hint: growing into an unwelcome heap (not *adding up*, *building up* or *stacking up*)

entries.related: *add up* — slowly reach a large total; *mount* — formal, increase, about costs or pressure; *build up* — increase gradually, often about stress or tension.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop working well and then fail completely, used about plans, deals, teams, relationships or organizations.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news: *The deal fell apart*, *Their marriage fell apart.* It describes something that existed or was working before and then collapses. It is intransitive; about a person, it means to lose emotional control (*She fell apart at the funeral*).
entries.pattern: a deal / marriage / team + falls apart
examples: The deal **fell apart** when the buyer couldn't get a mortgage.
Their marriage started to **fall apart** after he took a job in another state.
Our weekend plans **fell apart** when the babysitter canceled at the last minute.

drill.sentence: After the founder left, the company slowly {{fell apart}}, and it closed two years later.
drill.hint: stopped working and failed (not *went under*)

entries.related: *fall through* — a plan or deal does not happen; *go under* — a business goes bankrupt; *come apart at the seams* — informal, fail badly and visibly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be tricked into believing something that is not true, such as a lie, a joke or a scam.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *fall for a scam / a trick / a lie / it*, and especially *I can't believe I fell for that.* The object always follows *for*, even when it is a pronoun (*fall for it*). Don't confuse it with *fall for someone*, which means to fall in love with them.
entries.pattern: fall for + it / a trick / a scam / a line
examples: The email looked like it came from my bank, and I almost **fell for** it.
My dad **falls for** the same April Fools' joke every single year.
Thousands of people **fell for** the fake concert tickets sold on social media.

drill.sentence: Don't {{fall for}} those phone calls about a free cruise; they just want your credit card number.
drill.hint: believe them and get tricked (not *be fooled by*)

entries.related: *buy* — informal, believe a story (*I don't buy it*); *be taken in by* — be deceived; *see through* — the opposite, recognize a trick.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To belong to a particular group, category or class.
entries.usage: Common in explanations, reports and academic writing: *fall into three categories*, *fall into the high-risk group*. It is a bit more formal than *belong to* and often appears with a number when you divide something up. The subject is the things being classified, not the person who classifies them.
entries.pattern: fall into + two / three categories; fall into a group
examples: Most of the complaints we get **fall into** two categories: late deliveries and damaged boxes.
At seventy-two, my father now **falls into** the high-risk group for heat stroke.
The survey responses **fell into** three clear groups, depending on the participants' age.

drill.sentence: When it comes to pineapple on pizza, people tend to {{fall into}} two camps: they either love it or hate it.
drill.hint: each belong to one group or the other (not *split into*)

entries.related: *fall under* — be covered by a rule, a heading or someone's responsibility; *belong to* — plainer; *be classified as* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To use or fill an amount of time, space or attention.
entries.usage: Common in everyday talk about rooms, furniture and schedules: *take up space / room / time*, *take up half the garage*. In this sense the object almost always comes after *up* and is rarely a pronoun. *Take it up* usually means something else, such as starting a hobby or raising an issue with someone.
entries.pattern: take up + space / room / time / half the room
examples: The new couch is nice, but it **takes up** half the living room.
Driving the kids to practice **takes up** most of my Saturday.
I won't **take up** too much of your time — I just have two quick questions.

drill.sentence: We sold the piano because it {{took up}} so much space in our tiny apartment.
drill.hint: used, as its share of the room (not *ate up*)

mistake.wrong: The new bookshelf takes a lot of place.
mistake.right: The new bookshelf takes up a lot of space.
mistake.why: Things *take up space* or *room* in English; *place* means a location, and *take place* means *happen*.

entries.related: *eat up* — informal, use a lot of time or money; *occupy* — formal; *fill* — plainer.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To admit that something you said was wrong or unfair, and say that you no longer mean it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially *I take it back* and *I take back what I said*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*take it back*), while a longer object such as *what I said* follows *back*. It also means to return something to a store, so the context shows which meaning is meant.
entries.pattern: I take it back; take back what you said
examples: I said the movie would be boring, but I **take it back** — it was great.
He called my cooking bland, then quickly **took it back** when he saw my face.
You can't just **take back** something like that after saying it in front of everyone.

drill.sentence: Okay, I {{take back}} what I said about your brother; he was really helpful today.
drill.hint: withdraw, admitting it was wrong

entries.related: *retract* — formal, withdraw a statement; *eat your words* — informal, admit you were wrong; *stand by* — the opposite, keep supporting what you said.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To remove something that is hanging, standing or posted, such as a poster, a tent or a post online.
entries.usage: Used for decorations, signs, flags, tents and online content: *take down the Christmas lights*, *The video was taken down.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*take it down*); a noun can go before or after *down*. It also means to write something down, as in *take down someone's number*.
entries.pattern: take down + decorations / a tent / a post; be taken down
examples: We finally **took down** the Christmas lights in February.
The video was **taken down** within an hour because it broke the site's rules.
Can you help me **take the tent down** before it starts to rain?

drill.sentence: After the complaints, the restaurant {{took down}} the photo it had posted of a customer without permission.
drill.hint: made it disappear from its page (not *pulled* or *deleted*)

entries.related: *put up* — the opposite, hang or build something; *remove* — more formal; *pull* — informal, remove content or a product quickly.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To arrange to get a loan, mortgage or insurance policy from a bank or company.
entries.usage: Used in personal finance and news with a small set of objects: *take out a loan / a mortgage / insurance / a policy / an ad*. The object usually follows *out*; a pronoun goes in the middle (*take one out*). You take out a loan *from* a bank, but you *borrow* money *from* a friend.
entries.pattern: take out + a loan / a mortgage / insurance (from a bank)
examples: We **took out** a thirty-year mortgage when we bought the house.
She had to **take out** student loans to pay for nursing school.
Before the trip, I **took out** travel insurance in case anyone got sick.

drill.sentence: To pay for the new roof, they {{took out}} a loan from their credit union.
drill.hint: arranged to receive, as borrowers (not *applied for*)

entries.related: *borrow* — take money that you will pay back, more general; *pay off* — repay a loan completely; *apply for* — ask for a loan before it is approved.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To look or behave like an older relative, especially a parent or grandparent.
entries.usage: Very common in family conversation: *She takes after her mother.* It is a state verb, so it is rarely used in the progressive, and the relative always follows *after*. Unlike *look like*, it can describe character as well as looks (*He takes after his dad — always fixing things*).
entries.pattern: someone takes after + their mother / father / grandmother
examples: Everyone says I **take after** my grandfather — same nose, same terrible jokes.
Their son **takes after** his mother; he's calm and very organized.
She clearly **takes after** her dad when it comes to sports.

drill.sentence: With her red hair and quick temper, Maya really {{takes after}} her grandmother.
drill.hint: resembles an older relative, in looks and character (not *looks like*)

mistake.wrong: I take after my little sister on weekends when my parents work.
mistake.right: I look after my little sister on weekends when my parents work.
mistake.why: *Take after* means to resemble an older relative; *look after* means to take care of someone.

entries.related: *look like* — resemble in appearance only; *be the spitting image of* — look exactly like; *run in the family* — a trait many relatives share.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make a failing business, team or bad situation successful again.
entries.usage: Common in business and sports news and in personal stories: *turn the company around*, *turn things around*, *turn your life around*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*turn it around*), and the noun *turnaround* names the change. It can also be intransitive: *Their season turned around in October.*
entries.pattern: turn + a company / things / your life + around
examples: When she took over, the restaurant was losing money, but she **turned it around** in under a year.
He was failing three classes, but he **turned things around** and graduated on time.
Can a new coach **turn around** a team that hasn't won a game in two seasons?

drill.sentence: Volunteers opened a café in the empty bank building and helped {{turn around}} the whole neighborhood.
drill.hint: make it successful again (not *revive*)

entries.related: *bounce back* — recover by itself after a bad period; *get back on track* — return to the plan; *revive* — bring back to life, more formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think that you are better or more important than someone, and to treat them with little respect.
entries.usage: Used for attitudes about class, jobs, education and taste: *look down on people who …*, *look down on fast food*. It is critical and describes an attitude more than a single action. The object always follows *on*; the opposite is *look up to* (admire).
entries.pattern: look down on + someone / people who … / something
examples: Some of my classmates **looked down on** me because my parents didn't go to college.
Don't **look down on** fast-food jobs; they teach you a lot about pressure and teamwork.
He's such a wine snob that he **looks down on** anything that comes in a box.

drill.sentence: She grew up rich, but she never {{looked down on}} the kids from the other side of town.
drill.hint: saw as beneath her, socially

entries.related: *look up to* — the opposite, admire; *talk down to* — speak to someone as if they were stupid; *be a snob about* — think you have better taste than others.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think about something that happened in the past, often with a particular feeling about it.
entries.usage: Often used with a feeling or a judgment: *look back on those years fondly*, *When I look back on it, I laugh.* It is common in interviews, speeches and personal stories, and the past event always follows *on*. *Looking back* on its own is a frequent sentence opener: *Looking back, I should have quit sooner.*
entries.pattern: look back on + a time / an event (+ fondly / with regret)
examples: When I **look back on** my first year of teaching, I can't believe how nervous I was.
She **looks back on** her two years in Japan as the best of her life.
Someday we'll **look back on** this snowstorm and laugh.

drill.sentence: My parents {{look back on}} their first tiny apartment with a lot of affection.
drill.hint: think about from today's point of view (not *remember*)

entries.related: *reminisce about* — talk about happy memories; *dwell on* — keep thinking about something bad; *reflect on* — think about the past carefully and seriously.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To examine something fairly quickly to check that it is correct, complete or in good condition.
entries.usage: Common at work and in daily life with documents, cars, apartments and homework: *Could you look this over for me?* A pronoun goes in the middle (*look it over*), while a noun can go before or after *over*. It suggests a quick check; for a slower, line-by-line check, *go through* is more usual.
entries.pattern: look over + a document / a car; look it over
examples: My dad always **looks over** the check before he pays, just in case.
The mechanic **looked the car over** and said the brakes were fine.
My landlord **looked the apartment over** before giving back my deposit.

drill.sentence: I wrote a toast for my brother's wedding. Can you {{look it over}} and tell me if it's too long?
drill.hint: quickly check something for problems (not *go over it* or *read it over*)

entries.related: *go over* — check or explain something step by step; *go through* — examine carefully, one part at a time; *skim* — read quickly for the main points.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To refuse to accept unfair treatment from someone more powerful, and to resist them openly.
entries.usage: Used for bullies, bosses, parents and big organizations: *stand up to a bully*. It sounds positive and brave. Don't confuse it with *stand up for*, which means to defend or support someone else or a principle: *stand up for your little brother*.
entries.pattern: stand up to + a bully / your boss / a company
examples: My little sister finally **stood up to** the girl who'd been bullying her on the bus.
It takes courage to **stand up to** a boss who yells at people.
The small town **stood up to** the mining company and won in court.

drill.sentence: When the landlord tried to raise the rent again, the tenants got together and {{stood up to}} him.
drill.hint: resisted him openly, as a group

mistake.wrong: You have to stand up for bullies, or they'll never stop.
mistake.right: You have to stand up to bullies, or they'll never stop.
mistake.why: *Stand up to* someone means to resist them; *stand up for* someone means to defend or support them.

entries.related: *stand up for* — defend someone or something; *push back* — resist a demand or plan; *take on* — choose to fight or compete with a stronger opponent.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To believe in and support a set of values or principles, so that people connect you with them.
entries.usage: Common in talk about people, brands, schools and organizations: *What does she stand for?*, *stand for quality / fairness / something*. In this sense it is usually in the simple present. It also means to be short for (*NBA stands for National Basketball Association*) and, in negatives, to tolerate (*I won't stand for it*).
entries.pattern: stand for + values / quality / something; what X stands for
examples: I don't agree with all his views, but at least I know what he **stands for**.
Our family business has always **stood for** honest work at a fair price.
The coach wants the program to **stand for** hard work and respect, not just winning.

drill.sentence: Before you pick a college, find out what it really {{stands for}}, not just what it says in the brochure.
drill.hint: represents, in terms of values (not *believes in*)

entries.related: *believe in* — think something is right or important; *represent* — be a symbol of something; *stand by* — keep supporting a decision or a person.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To continue doing or using something, instead of changing to something else or giving up.
entries.usage: Common in everyday decisions: *stick with the plan / the original color / your gut / the same phone company*. It suggests keeping something although you could change, often after some doubt or difficulty. *Stick with someone* means to stay with or support a person; for rules, diets and promises, *stick to* is more usual.
entries.pattern: stick with + a plan / a choice / it
examples: We thought about switching to a cheaper phone plan, but we **stuck with** the one we had.
Piano was hard at first, but I'm glad I **stuck with** it.
If the recipe works, **stick with** it — don't change three things at once.

drill.sentence: The new coach wants to change everything, but most players would rather {{stick with}} the system that won them a title.
drill.hint: keep using instead of changing — verb + *with* (not *stay with*)

entries.related: *stick to* — keep to a rule, plan, diet or promise; *stay with* — continue with, very close in meaning; *give up* — the opposite, stop trying.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To keep something and not lose, sell or give it away.
entries.usage: Common with money, possessions, jobs, a lead and hope: *hold on to your receipt*, *hold on to the lead*. American English often writes it *hold onto*, and a pronoun goes after the preposition (*hold on to it*). The literal meaning is to keep holding something with your hands.
entries.pattern: hold on to + a receipt / the lead / hope / it
examples: **Hold on to** your receipt in case the shoes don't fit.
They **held on to** a one-goal lead for the last twenty minutes of the game.
My parents **held on to** their old farmhouse for years, even though nobody lived there.

drill.sentence: If I were you, I'd {{hold on to}} those shares for a few more years instead of selling now.
drill.hint: avoid selling or giving away (not *hang on to*)

entries.related: *hang on to* — same meaning, more informal; *keep* — plainer; *let go of* — the opposite, stop holding or stop trying to keep.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To help a person or organization out of financial trouble, usually by giving or lending money.
entries.usage: Common in news about banks and companies, and in family talk: *My parents had to bail me out.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*bail them out*), and the noun is *bailout* (*a government bailout*). It can sound critical, suggesting the person caused the problem themselves.
entries.pattern: bail someone out (with a loan); a bailout
examples: When I lost my job, my sister **bailed me out** with a loan for rent.
The government **bailed out** several large banks during the 2008 financial crisis.
Every time he gets into debt, his parents **bail him out**, so he never learns.

drill.sentence: The local soccer club was nearly bankrupt until a businessman {{bailed it out}} with two million dollars.
drill.hint: rescued it with money (not *saved it*)

entries.related: *help out* — help in a general way; *rescue* — save from danger or failure; *prop up* — keep a weak company or system going with support.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop pressuring, threatening or criticizing someone, and give them space.
entries.usage: Informal and very direct: as a command (*Back off!*) it can sound rude or aggressive. In calmer use it describes someone choosing to stop pushing: *I backed off and let her decide.* Compare *back down*, which means to give up a demand or an argument.
entries.pattern: back off (a little / a bit); tell someone to back off
examples: My mom kept asking when I'd get married, so I finally told her to **back off**.
**Back off**, okay? I said I'd finish it tonight.
Once the coach **backed off** a little, the players started enjoying the game again.

drill.sentence: My in-laws give us advice about the baby all day long; I wish they'd {{back off}} a bit.
drill.hint: stop pushing and give us space (not *ease up*, *let up* or *lay off*)

entries.related: *back down* — give up a demand or position; *lay off* — informal, stop criticizing or annoying someone; *ease up* — become less strict or intense.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To hide a mistake, a crime or an embarrassing fact so that other people do not find out about it.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about scandals: *cover up a crime / a mistake / the truth*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*cover it up*), and the noun *cover-up* is an attempt to hide something. It always suggests dishonesty, unless it is used literally for putting something over something.
entries.pattern: cover up + a mistake / a crime / the truth; a cover-up
examples: The manager tried to **cover up** the accident, but a customer had recorded it on her phone.
She **covered up** her mistake by blaming the printer.
Investigators say the company **covered up** safety problems for years.

drill.sentence: He spilled coffee on the white couch and tried to {{cover it up}} with a cushion before his wife got home.
drill.hint: hide what happened (not *conceal it*)

entries.related: *hush up* — keep something quiet so the public doesn't hear; *sweep under the rug* — ignore a problem and hope nobody notices; *conceal* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To explain something or solve a misunderstanding, so that it is no longer confusing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and work emails: *clear up a misunderstanding / some confusion / a few questions*, *Let me clear that up.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*clear it up*). Without an object, the weather or an illness can also *clear up*.
entries.pattern: clear up + a misunderstanding / confusion; clear that up
examples: Thanks for calling — that **clears up** a lot of confusion about the schedule.
There's been a misunderstanding, and I'd like to **clear it up** before Monday.
The receipt **cleared things up**: she had paid, and the store's system was wrong.

drill.sentence: My neighbor thought I had parked in her spot, but we {{cleared it up}} over coffee.
drill.hint: settled the misunderstanding (not *sorted it out*, *worked it out* or *straightened it out*)

entries.related: *sort out* — solve a problem or a mess; *straighten out* — correct a confusion or a mistake; *clarify* — formal, make clearer.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To prepare and write a formal or detailed document, such as a contract, plan, list or agreement.
entries.usage: Used at work, in law and in planning: *draw up a contract / a will / a plan / a list / a budget*. It suggests careful preparation of an official or detailed text, not a quick note. The object usually follows *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle (*draw it up*).
entries.pattern: draw up + a contract / a will / a plan / a list
examples: Our lawyer is **drawing up** the contract, so we should be able to sign next week.
Before the wedding, we **drew up** a list of everyone we absolutely had to invite.
My parents finally **drew up** a will after a friend of theirs died without one.

drill.sentence: The city has hired consultants to {{draw up}} a plan for new bike lanes downtown.
drill.hint: prepare in writing (not *put together* or *write up*)

entries.related: *write up* — turn notes into a full report; *put together* — prepare by combining parts, more general; *draft* — write a first version.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To get rid of a rule, system, practice or tradition, so that it no longer exists.
entries.usage: Common in news and talk about change: *do away with fees / paper tickets / the dress code*. The subject is usually an institution or someone in charge, and the passive is common (*The rule was done away with*). It sounds neutral; *abolish* and *eliminate* are more formal.
entries.pattern: do away with + a rule / fees / a tradition
examples: Our office **did away with** assigned desks, so now you sit wherever there's space.
Many airlines have **done away with** free checked bags.
The school **did away with** its strict dress code after students complained for years.

drill.sentence: The restaurant {{did away with}} tipping and raised its prices by twenty percent instead.
drill.hint: ended the practice of (not *got rid of* or *scrapped*)

entries.related: *get rid of* — more general and informal; *scrap* — informal, cancel a plan or system; *abolish* — formal, end a law or system officially.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To accept that an unpleasant fact or situation exists and start dealing with it, instead of avoiding it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about personal problems and in news about institutions: *face up to the facts / the problem / your mistakes*. It suggests something you have been avoiding for a while. *Face* alone is also possible, but *face up to* stresses the honesty and courage it takes.
entries.pattern: face up to + the fact that … / a problem / your mistakes
examples: At some point, you have to **face up to** the fact that the relationship is over.
The company needs to **face up to** its mistakes instead of blaming its customers.
He finally **faced up to** his drinking problem and joined a support group.

drill.sentence: My dad refused to {{face up to}} his hearing loss until he missed a call from the hospital.
drill.hint: accept and deal with (not *come to terms with*)

entries.related: *come to terms with* — slowly accept something sad; *own up to* — admit you did something wrong; *bury your head in the sand* — the opposite, refuse to see a problem.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be successful in your career or life, especially by doing better than other people.
entries.usage: Common in talk about work, education and money: *get ahead in life / at work / in business*. It often suggests competition and can sound slightly critical (*She'd do anything to get ahead*). *Get ahead of someone* means to move in front of them or do better than them.
entries.pattern: get ahead (in life / at work / in business)
examples: My parents each worked two jobs so that we could **get ahead** in life.
In this industry, it's hard to **get ahead** without knowing the right people.
He'll do anything to **get ahead**, even take credit for other people's work.

drill.sentence: Learning a second language can really help you {{get ahead}} in international business.
drill.hint: succeed and advance (not *move up*)

entries.related: *move up* — get a higher position; *climb the ladder* — rise step by step in a career; *fall behind* — the opposite, make less progress than others.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To avoid doing something that you should do or have agreed to do.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *get out of doing the dishes / a meeting / jury duty / a contract*. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form after *of* and often suggests an excuse or a trick. *Try to get out of* and *There's no getting out of it* are frequent combinations.
entries.pattern: get out of + -ing / a duty / a contract
examples: He always finds a way to **get out of** doing the dishes.
Is there any way to **get out of** jury duty if you're traveling that week?
We signed a two-year contract, so we can't **get out of** it without paying a fee.

drill.sentence: My brother faked a cough to {{get out of}} his piano lesson, but my mom wasn't fooled.
drill.hint: avoid having to go to (not *skip*)

entries.related: *skip* — not go to something; *wriggle out of* — escape a duty in a clever, dishonest way; *back out of* — withdraw from something you agreed to.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To reveal a secret or information, often by accident, through what you say or how you act.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about secrets, surprises, card games and movies: *give away the ending*, *Her smile gave it away.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*give it away*), and *give yourself away* means to show your secret without meaning to. A *dead giveaway* is a clear sign that reveals something.
entries.pattern: give away + the ending / a secret; give it / yourself away
examples: Don't tell Dad about the party — he'll **give it away** by smiling too much.
The trailer **gives away** the whole plot, so don't watch it.
She said she was fine, but her red eyes **gave her away**.

drill.sentence: We were planning a surprise party, but my little cousin {{gave it away}} by asking my mom what flavor her birthday cake would be.
drill.hint: revealed the secret by accident (not *let it slip*)

entries.related: *let something slip* — say something secret by accident; *spill the beans* — informal, reveal a secret; *spoil* — reveal the ending of a story.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give something to someone, or give them control of or responsibility for something, often because you are asked or ordered to.
entries.usage: Used literally (*hand over your keys*) and for control and responsibility (*hand the business over to her son*). A pronoun goes in the middle (*hand it over*), and *to* names the new person. In news it often suggests an order or force: *The robbers made him hand over the cash.*
entries.pattern: hand over + keys / control / a business (to someone); hand it over
examples: When my dad retired, he **handed the farm over** to my older brother.
The officer asked him to **hand over** his license and registration.
Before your vacation, please **hand over** your open cases to Jen.

drill.sentence: The kids refused to {{hand over}} the TV remote until their show was finished.
drill.hint: pass to someone else (not *give up*)

entries.related: *pass on* — give something to the next person; *turn over* — give to the authorities; *take over* — the opposite side, take control from someone.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To ask an outside person, such as an expert or a consultant, to join a group or a job to help with something.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports and in news: *bring in an expert / a consultant / a specialist / the police*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*bring her in*), while a longer noun usually follows *in*. It suggests that the group could not solve the problem alone.
entries.pattern: bring in + an expert / a consultant / a new coach
examples: The school **brought in** a counselor to talk to students after the accident.
When sales kept dropping, the owners **brought in** a consultant from New York.
The team **brought in** a new coach halfway through the season.

drill.sentence: Our dog wouldn't stop chewing the furniture, so we finally {{brought in}} a professional trainer.
drill.hint: hired from outside to help (not *called in*)

entries.related: *call in* — ask an expert or the police to come and help, often urgently; *hire* — give someone a job; *take on* — hire new staff or accept new work.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To reduce the level of something, such as prices, costs, numbers or a fever.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and health: *bring down prices / costs / unemployment / a fever*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*bring it down*), and a noun can go before or after *down*. *Bring down* can also mean to make a government or leader lose power.
entries.pattern: bring down + prices / costs / a fever; bring it down
examples: The new factory should help **bring down** the price of electric cars.
Opening a second checkout lane **brought the wait time down** to about five minutes.
Buying in bulk has **brought down** our grocery bill by about a hundred dollars a month.

drill.sentence: Cutting back on salt helped my dad {{bring down}} his blood pressure.
drill.hint: make it fall to a healthier level (not *lower* or *reduce*)

entries.related: *cut* — reduce, often by a decision; *drive down* — push prices or costs lower; *lower* — plainer; *push up* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To formally and publicly ask a person or organization to do something.
entries.usage: Typical of news, official statements and speeches. The pattern is almost always *call on someone to do something*, and *call upon* is even more formal. In a classroom, *call on someone* means to ask a student to answer.
entries.pattern: call on + someone + to do something
examples: The mayor **called on** residents to save water during the heat wave.
Parents are **calling on** the school board to bring back the late bus.
The report **calls on** airlines to give passengers clearer information about delays.

drill.sentence: After the bridge collapse, engineers {{called on}} the state to inspect every bridge built before 1970.
drill.hint: formally and publicly asked (not *urged*)

entries.related: *urge* — strongly advise, also formal; *appeal to* — ask someone for help or support; *call for* — demand that something happens (*call for an inquiry*).

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To not include something or someone, either on purpose or by mistake.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *leave out a detail / a name / the onions*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*leave it out*), and *feel left out* means to feel excluded by a group. *Omit* is the formal written equivalent.
entries.pattern: leave out + a detail / a name / an ingredient; feel left out
examples: Can you **leave out** the onions? My son won't eat them.
You **left out** the most important part of the story — did she say yes?
When I booked the flight, I **left out** my middle name, and now the airline says my ticket doesn't match my passport.

drill.sentence: When she told her parents about the trip, she {{left out}} the part where they got lost in the desert at night.
drill.hint: didn't include in her story (not *skipped* or *glossed over*)

entries.related: *omit* — formal; *skip* — not do or mention a part; *include* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To suggest a plan, idea, name or theory so that other people can discuss it or decide on it.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, committees and news: *put forward a proposal / an idea / a theory / a candidate*. It sounds a bit more formal than *suggest*. A pronoun or a short name goes in the middle (*put it forward*, *put her name forward*), but a long noun phrase comes after *forward*.
entries.pattern: put forward + an idea / a proposal / a theory / a name
examples: Several neighbors **put forward** ideas for the empty lot, from a garden to a basketball court.
She **put her name forward** for the board of the local food bank.
The idea of continental drift was **put forward** in 1912 but wasn't widely accepted for decades.

drill.sentence: At the family meeting, my sister {{put forward}} the idea of selling the cabin.
drill.hint: suggested for everyone to discuss (not *brought up*)

entries.related: *bring up* — mention a topic for discussion; *propose* — more formal; *float* — informal, suggest an idea to see how people react.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To spend time, work or effort on something, often a lot of it.
entries.usage: Common in talk about work, sports and study: *put in the hours / the time / the work / a lot of effort*. A long amount usually comes after *in* (*put in sixty-hour weeks*), while short objects often go in the middle (*put the work in*). *Put in a request* or *an order* is a different meaning: to submit it.
entries.pattern: put in + hours / time / work / effort; put the work in
examples: She **put in** sixty-hour weeks for a year to get the restaurant off the ground.
If you want to run a marathon, you have to **put the miles in**.
We **put in** a lot of work on this garden, so please keep the dog out of it.

drill.sentence: He's only been here a year, but he's {{put in}} more hours than anyone else on the team.
drill.hint: spent working (not *logged* or *worked*)

entries.related: *devote* — give time or energy to something, more formal; *invest* — put time or money in, hoping for a result; *log* — record hours worked or traveled.
